title: Advantages and disadvantages at a national level

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Weigh the advantages and disadvantages specialisation at a national level brings to consumers, firms and the economy, and answer questions set in a context.

blocks.heading: Who gains what
blocks.text: The advantages land on three parties. Consumers gain variety and price: goods the country does not make arrive through trade and tend to cost less than home production at a higher cost per unit. Firms gain scale: selling abroad lets a specialist firm produce larger quantities, which lowers the cost per unit further - flower growers in the Netherlands sell far beyond their home market. The economy gains export revenue, jobs and skills in the specialised sector.

blocks.heading: The risk of a narrow base
blocks.text: The disadvantages grow from how narrow the specialisation is. Where a large share of export revenue rests on a single product, a fall in its world price cuts earnings sharply. Take a country earning N$4 000 million from exports, with N$3 200 million of it from one crop: a fall of a fifth in the crop's price takes the revenue down to N$2 560 million, with the tonnage unchanged. Workers in the sector feel the change first, and the economy has less for imports.

blocks.heading: Disadvantages for consumers and firms
blocks.text:
The risk of a narrow base falls on the economy as a whole, but specialisation also carries disadvantages for consumers and for firms.

Consumers: a country that specialises buys many of its goods from abroad, so its consumers depend on imports. When supply is disrupted - by a war, a drought in the exporting country, a port closure, a shipping delay or an export ban - goods may run short and prices rise. In 2022 the war in Ukraine, a large exporter of wheat and sunflower oil, pushed up the price of bread flour and cooking oil in many importing countries, southern Africa included. A fall in the exchange rate also makes imported goods dearer at once. And where home producers have closed, consumers lose the choice of goods made locally.

Firms: specialised exporters sell into world markets they do not control. When world demand falls or a buyer country raises a tariff, their sales and prices tend to fall together, as a Walvis Bay fish processor finds when European demand weakens. Firms that rely on imported inputs - machinery, fuel, packaging - face higher costs or delays when supplies are disrupted or the currency falls. Firms making goods the country no longer specialises in face foreign rivals producing at a lower cost per unit, and some may be forced to close, taking jobs with them.

blocks.heading: General or the context
blocks.text: The confusion learners make: a question set in a context is answered with the advantages of specialisation in general, without touching the information provided. The boundary: the general advantages name what tends to happen where a country specialises; the context asks what those tendencies mean for the economy in the extract, with its figures and products. The test: each point should use something the extract states - a figure, a firm, a product. Where a point could sit under any question about specialisation, it needs the extract's evidence first.

blocks.heading: How the balance is struck
blocks.text: How far the advantages outweigh the disadvantages tends to turn on the spread of the exports and the ease of shifting resources. Revenue from several products carries a smaller risk than revenue resting on a single crop, because a price fall in one product is then a smaller share of the whole. Where workers and equipment can move, a lasting fall in demand costs less.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The free trade that carries a specialised country's exports is examined in topic 6.2, and the exchange-rate changes that move what those exports earn in topic 6.3.
